html:
Kumis is fermented mare's milk, a slightly sour, mildly alcoholic drink of the Eurasian steppe. The Greek historian Herodotus described the Scythians making it in the 5th century BCE, and people across the steppe still drink it.

Herodotus wrote that the Scythians stirred the milk in wooden tubs to separate the best part, and he told a grim story that they blinded their slaves to do the work. Fresh mare's milk is too rich in sugar to drink much of; fermenting it in leather bags or wooden tubs, with steady churning, turns it into a drink that keeps.

Milking mares may be very old. Traces of mare's milk fat in pots of the Botai culture of Kazakhstan, from around 3500 BCE, have been linked to the early days of horse domestication.

The drink appears again and again in history. The friar William of Rubruck tasted it at the Mongol court in the 1250s and said it went down pleasantly. Today it is a national drink in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Mongolia, where it is called airag.
